strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored setting: long surveillance-video search with image+text queries and temporally grounded answers. This is a realistic forensic workflow that is not well covered by standard long-video QA benchmarks.

ForeSeaQA is a potentially useful benchmark contribution. It combines multiple-choice QA, multimodal person-reference queries, and timestamped evidence across several surveillance-oriented subtasks, which is a meaningful step beyond text-only or answer-only evaluation.

The proposed system is simple, modular, and practical: person tracking narrows the search space, a multimodal retriever handles image/text queries, and a Video LMM performs final reasoning. This makes the approach easy to understand and likely implementable with existing components.

The experimental section is reasonably broad, with comparisons to several Video LMMs and VideoRAG-style baselines, ablations over spatial grounding and top-K retrieval, retrieval analysis, latency measurements, and some evidence of transfer to open-domain long-video benchmarks.
weaknesses: The main algorithmic contribution is limited. ForeSea is largely a composition of off-the-shelf tracking, VISTA/GCL-style multimodal retrieval, and VideoLLaMA3 generation. The strongest contribution is better viewed as Datasets/Benchmarks plus Applied/Systems rather than a novel algorithm; under that framing the benchmark quality becomes central, but it is not documented rigorously enough.

ForeSeaQA is small for a benchmark claim: 1,041 questions derived from UCF-Crime and dense captions. The paper does not provide enough detail on video/question splits, annotation protocol, number and expertise of human validators, inter-annotator agreement, rejection rates, or examples of corrected/generated failures.

The dataset construction relies heavily on LLM-generated captions, LLM-generated QA, and LMM-based visual grounding. Even with manual verification, this raises concerns about inherited caption biases, hallucinated events, shallow answer patterns, and benchmark artifacts. The paper does not include artifact analysis, human performance, random-choice/language-only baselines, or leakage checks.

The empirical gains are modest in the main table. ForeSea improves average accuracy over VideoLLaMA3 by only 1.4 points and average temporal IoU by only 0.4 points, while absolute IoU remains very low at 13.6%. This weakens the claim that the system provides precise temporal grounding.

Some results complicate the central person-centric story. ForeSea-Global appears stronger than ForeSea on temporal IoU in the appendix, and Qwen2.5-VL-72B has higher multimodal IoU than ForeSea in Table 1. The paper does not fully reconcile these cases with the claimed advantage of person-centric retrieval.

The open-domain benchmark comparison is not fully convincing. Many numbers are reported from original papers, while ForeSea is evaluated under its own frame budget and retrieval setup; this may not be an apples-to-apples comparison. The adaptation from person-centric clips to uniform frame indexing also changes the method substantially.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The supplement provides generation prompts, but key details such as exact tracker/detector settings, embedding checkpoints, prompt templates for inference, hardware, index construction time, and database statistics are not sufficiently specified.

The surveillance/forensic application has significant privacy, bias, and misuse risks, especially with person search from images. The paper gives little discussion of consent, demographic bias, false identification risk, deployment boundaries, or safeguards. For this domain, that omission is scientifically and socially important.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem: multimodal forensic search over long surveillance videos with both answer prediction and temporal grounding.

The contribution is best viewed as a Dataset/Benchmarks plus Applied/Systems paper, rather than an Algorithms/General paper. Under that framing, the idea of pairing reference images with surveillance QA and timestamped evidence is potentially useful.
The manuscript evaluates a reasonably broad set of recent Video LMMs and retrieval-augmented baselines, and includes ablations on retrieval design choices, top-K, spatial cues, and latency.
The supplementary material provides prompt templates and additional subtask-level results, which helps clarify the dataset generation and evaluation procedure.
weaknesses: The main technical method is mostly a straightforward composition of off-the-shelf tracking, multimodal embedding, retrieval, and VideoLMM prompting. The paper repeatedly claims a novel system, but the algorithmic contribution is quite limited.

The empirical gains are modest and do not convincingly support the strong claims. ForeSea improves average accuracy only slightly over VideoLLaMA3, and temporal IoU remains very low overall. In the text setting, VideoLLaMA3 has higher accuracy than ForeSea, while the supplementary ForeSea-Global variant often outperforms the main method on IoU, making the claimed person-centric advantage less clean.

The benchmark construction raises substantial concerns. QA pairs and timestamps are generated from dense captions using LLMs, so the benchmark may reflect caption artifacts rather than true video understanding. The paper gives too little detail on manual verification scale, annotator expertise, agreement, rejection rates, quality control, and whether timestamps are complete and precise.

The dataset is small for a benchmark paper: 1,041 questions from UCF-Crime, with an emphasized search category. This limits statistical reliability and makes it hard to assess generalization across surveillance scenarios, camera types, and event distributions.

The evaluation protocol is underspecified in important places: prompts, decoding settings, frame budgets for all baselines, handling of output-format failures, confidence intervals, and significance testing are missing. The negative-search IoU convention, where both negative prediction and negative ground truth receive IoU=1, can also inflate localization scores.

The open-domain benchmark comparison is not fully convincing. Table 4 reports many numbers from original papers rather than a controlled reimplementation, while ForeSea changes its database construction to frame-level indexing, weakening the connection to the proposed surveillance/person-centric method.

Several claims are overstated, especially “first” and “state-of-the-art” claims. The related work discussion does not sufficiently distinguish this benchmark from recent multimodal temporal retrieval and surveillance VQA datasets, nor does it justify why existing datasets cannot be adapted to similar queries.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper does not clearly specify dataset release status, splits, raw annotations, code release, hardware, detector configuration, tracking failure handling, or licensing/ethical constraints for surveillance-derived crops.

The societal and privacy implications are underdeveloped for a surveillance forensic-search system. Given the domain, the paper should discuss misuse, identity tracking, bias, consent, false accusations, and safeguards much more seriously.

Presentation quality is uneven, with formatting issues, cramped tables, inconsistent naming, and some unclear wording. These do not alone determine the decision, but they compound the larger concerns about rigor and evidential strength.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important gap: long surveillance-video QA with image+text queries and temporal evidence. ForeSeaQA is a valuable benchmark contribution because it combines multimodal person-reference queries, multiple forensic subtasks, and timestamped evidence rather than only answer accuracy.

The proposed ForeSea system is simple but well matched to the problem. Person-centric tracking plus multimodal retrieval is a sensible inductive bias for forensic search, and the plug-and-play design makes the approach relatively easy to reproduce and extend with stronger trackers, retrievers, or VideoLLMs.

The experimental section is broad: the paper compares multiple VideoLLMs, retrieval-augmented baselines, text-only and multimodal settings, latency, retrieval backbones, ablations, and transfer to general long-video benchmarks. The ablations are especially useful in showing when person-centric retrieval helps and when global retrieval may be better.

The empirical results support the main claim that current VideoLLMs struggle with multimodal forensic queries and temporal grounding. ForeSea gives the best multimodal accuracy on ForeSeaQA and is more efficient than the retrieval baselines, which is meaningful for the intended application.
The supplementary material provides prompt templates and additional subtask/retrieval results, improving transparency for the benchmark construction process.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty of ForeSea is limited. The system is largely a composition of existing components: ByteTrack/YOLO, a VISTA/GCL-style multimodal encoder, and VideoLLaMA3. This is acceptable for a benchmark/systems contribution, but the paper sometimes frames the pipeline more strongly than its technical originality warrants.

The absolute temporal grounding performance remains low. ForeSea obtains 13.6% average IoU on ForeSeaQA, and many non-search subtasks have very low IoU. This weakens claims about precise temporal grounding and suggests that the benchmark is still far from solved even by the proposed method.

The gains over the strongest non-retrieval VideoLLM are modest: ForeSea improves overall accuracy from 64.6 to 66.0 and IoU from 13.2 to 13.6 relative to VideoLLaMA3 in Table 1. The larger claimed gains mainly hold against prior RAG baselines, which are not always the strongest competitors.

The benchmark construction relies heavily on generated dense captions and LLM-based entity/QA generation before manual verification. The paper does not provide enough detail on annotator count, agreement, rejection rates, quality-control protocol, or whether caption-derived biases make the QA easier or less representative of raw forensic video understanding.

ForeSeaQA has only 1,041 curated questions from UCF-Crime, which is useful but relatively small for a new benchmark. The paper would be stronger with clearer discussion of dataset splits, diversity of scenes/cameras, licensing/privacy considerations, and robustness to tracker failures or occlusions.

Some evaluation choices need clearer justification. The IoU convention that assigns 1 when both prediction and ground truth are negative can inflate search-task localization scores, and multimodal evaluation excludes counting/anomaly tasks, making averages across text and multimodal settings somewhat hard to interpret.

The open-domain benchmark comparisons rely partly on numbers from original papers, which may involve different inference settings. This is encouraging evidence of generality but less convincing than a fully controlled re-evaluation under matched models, frames, prompts, and decoding settings.

The paper is surveillance-focused but has little discussion of societal risks, privacy, misuse, or deployment constraints. Given the forensic-search framing and person-centric indexing, a more substantial limitations and responsible-use discussion is important.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored computer vision problem: forensic search over long surveillance videos with image-plus-text queries and temporally grounded answers. This is better assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks plus Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic paper, since the main value is ForeSeaQA and a practical retrieval pipeline built from existing components.

ForeSeaQA has a clear task definition that combines multiple-choice QA with temporal localization, and the inclusion of multimodal person-reference queries is well motivated by realistic surveillance workflows. The six subtasks cover search, activity, event, temporal, counting, and anomaly questions, which gives the benchmark more breadth than simple retrieval or QA-only datasets.

The dataset construction pipeline is described reasonably well, including entity extraction from dense captions, LMM-based grounding, QA generation, and two-stage manual/automatic verification. The supplementary material provides prompt templates and metric definitions, which helps reproducibility.

The ForeSea system is simple but sensible: person tracking reduces the search space, a multimodal encoder supports text and image-text retrieval, and a VideoLMM answers using retrieved clips plus timestamp/bounding-box metadata. The person-centric retrieval bias is appropriate for the surveillance setting.

The experiments are fairly broad. The paper compares against several Video LMMs and RAG baselines, reports both text-only and multimodal query settings, includes ablations over spatial cues, top-K retrieval, global/person/hybrid retrieval, encoders, and VLM backbones, and also studies latency.

The reported results support the main claim that retrieval improves temporal grounding: ForeSea improves over prior RAG baselines on ForeSeaQA and the hybrid/global variants reach higher temporal IoU, while maintaining competitive accuracy and lower inference latency.
weaknesses: The system-level novelty is modest. ForeSea is largely a composition of ByteTrack/YOLO, existing multimodal encoders, and an existing VideoLMM. The main methodological insight, person-centric retrieval for surveillance QA, is useful but not technically deep enough by itself for a strong algorithmic contribution.

The benchmark is relatively small at 1,041 questions and is derived from UCF-Crime plus dense captions. This raises concerns about diversity, scalability, and whether models can exploit caption-generation artifacts or dataset-specific biases rather than robust visual reasoning.

The data generation process depends heavily on LLM/LMM-produced captions, entity extraction, grounding, and QA generation. Although manual verification is mentioned, the paper does not provide enough detail on annotator protocol, inter-annotator agreement, correction rates by task, quality-control criteria, or remaining label noise.

There is a possible circularity/leakage issue: ForeSeaQA is generated from UCA dense captions, and an oracle-caption baseline achieves very high accuracy. The benchmark may partly measure consistency with generated captions rather than independent human-defined forensic intent. Stronger human-authored queries or an independently annotated subset would make the dataset claim more convincing.

Absolute temporal localization remains low. The main ForeSea result reports only 13.6% average IoU, and even improved hybrid variants remain around 18-20% in supplementary tables. This supports the claim that the task is hard, but it also limits the practical usefulness of the current system as a forensic search tool.

The open-domain generalization evidence is weaker than the ForeSeaQA evaluation. Results on VideoMME/MLVU are mostly compared to numbers reported from original papers, and the retrieval/indexing setup differs from the surveillance pipeline. This makes claims of broad generality less convincing.

Important reproducibility and fairness details are missing or thin, including exact inference prompts for timestamp extraction, how malformed temporal outputs are parsed, frame sampling policies for all baselines, hardware/batching assumptions for latency, and whether all methods receive comparable visual evidence budgets.

The paper lacks a serious discussion of privacy, misuse, consent, and bias risks, which is especially important for surveillance and forensic search. This omission is not just cosmetic: deployment claims in this domain require careful treatment of false positives, identity errors, and potential harms.

Some claims are overstated. Phrases such as first system or first benchmark may be plausible within the paper's scope, but the related-work boundary is narrow and the benchmark comparison table compresses important differences across tasks, annotations, query types, and domains.

strengths: The paper targets an important and under-served problem: forensic search over long surveillance videos with image-plus-text queries and timestamped evidence. This is a relevant computer vision setting, and the benchmark framing is potentially useful if released and validated carefully.

The proposed system is simple and practical: tracking-based person-centric segmentation, multimodal retrieval, and a VideoLMM reader. The ablations show that retrieval scope, spatial cues, and top-K choices affect accuracy/localization, and the supplement provides useful subtask-level breakdowns.
The manuscript compares against several VideoLMMs and retrieval-augmented baselines, and reports both answer accuracy and temporal IoU rather than only multiple-choice accuracy.
weaknesses: The scientific case is not convincing. The method itself is mostly a composition of off-the-shelf tracking, multimodal embedding, and VideoLMM components; the main algorithmic novelty is limited, and the strongest contribution would need to be the benchmark. However, the benchmark evidence is not strong enough to support the large claims.

ForeSeaQA is small for a benchmark claim: only 1,041 questions derived from UCF-Crime. The generation pipeline relies heavily on dense captions and LLMs, with temporal labels selected from caption timestamps. Manual verification is described only vaguely, with no annotator protocol, agreement, quality statistics, failure rates by task, or release/licensing details.

There is a serious risk of circularity and shortcut learning in the benchmark construction. Questions, answers, distractors, and timestamps are generated from captions, and the oracle-caption baseline reaches 83.2% accuracy. This suggests much of the benchmark may reflect caption-derived semantics rather than independently verified video understanding. The paper does not sufficiently disentangle visual grounding from caption artifacts.

The reported gains are modest and sometimes internally undercut the claims. In Table 1, ForeSea improves overall accuracy over VideoLLaMA3 from 64.6 to 66.0 and IoU from 13.2 to 13.6, which is small. The main claimed IoU gain is mainly over weaker RAG baselines whose retrieval/localization behavior may not be well adapted to this task. Temporal IoU remains very low overall, so claims of precise or strong temporal grounding are overstated.

The paper’s choice of default method is confusing: ForeSea-Global and ForeSea-Hybrid in the ablations/supplement often outperform the reported ForeSea default on IoU and/or accuracy. This weakens the clarity of the contribution and makes the main-table comparison feel selectively framed.

The evaluation lacks key controls: no statistical significance or confidence intervals, unclear train/test or video split details, no analysis of overlap between query images and indexed clips, limited discussion of negative examples, and no robust evaluation of whether models exploit multiple-choice priors or dataset generation artifacts.

The open-domain benchmark comparison is not rigorous. The table states that many numbers are taken from original papers, while ForeSea is evaluated under its own retrieval setting. This is not a controlled comparison and should not be used to claim broad generalization or state-of-the-art behavior.

Efficiency claims appear incomplete because database construction, tracking, detection, embedding, and indexing costs are not fully accounted for. In a surveillance setting, these costs are central to practical deployment.

The paper handles a sensitive surveillance/forensic application but provides essentially no meaningful societal impact, privacy, bias, misuse, or deployment-risk analysis. For this domain, that omission is substantial.

Presentation quality is uneven, with grammatical issues and occasional unclear terminology. More importantly, several claims such as 'first', 'precise temporal grounding', and 'significant gains' are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important gap: multimodal forensic search over long surveillance videos with both answer prediction and temporal grounding. The task formulation is well motivated by realistic image+text queries such as identifying a person from a reference crop and localizing relevant events.

ForeSeaQA is a valuable benchmark contribution. It includes 1,041 manually verified questions over long UCF-Crime videos, covers six subtasks, supports both text-only and image+text query modes, and evaluates temporal localization in addition to multiple-choice accuracy. The dataset design is meaningfully different from standard long-video QA benchmarks.

The proposed ForeSea pipeline is simple but appropriate: tracking reduces the search space, multimodal retrieval handles image+text queries, and a VideoLMM reasons over the retrieved clips. This is a credible and reproducible system-level contribution rather than an unnecessarily complex new model.

The empirical evaluation is broad. The authors compare against multiple Video LMMs and retrieval-augmented baselines, report accuracy and temporal IoU, include detailed subtask analysis, ablate spatial grounding choices, retrieval top-K, encoders, VLM backbones, and evaluate transfer to general long-video benchmarks.

Results support the main claims: ForeSea improves ForeSeaQA average accuracy over strong 7B baselines and improves temporal IoU substantially over prior RAG baselines; the hybrid/global variants further show that person-centric and scene-level retrieval provide complementary evidence.

The paper is generally clear and transparent about the data engine, prompt templates, implementation details, and the remaining difficulty of temporal grounding and counting. The supplementary material improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate. ForeSea mainly composes existing tracking, multimodal embedding, and VideoLMM components. This is acceptable for an applied/benchmark-style contribution, but the paper sometimes frames the system contribution more strongly than the technical novelty warrants.

The dataset is relatively small at 1,041 questions and is derived from UCF-Crime plus dense captions and LLM-generated QA. Although manual verification is reported, the paper does not provide enough detail on annotator protocol, inter-annotator agreement, rejection criteria, or how temporal boundary quality was validated.

Because QA generation relies on dense captions and extracted person entities, there is a risk that the benchmark inherits captioning biases or misses visual details absent from captions. The oracle-caption baseline reaching 83.2% accuracy suggests that much of the benchmark may be solvable from high-quality captions, even if temporal localization remains challenging.

Absolute temporal grounding performance remains low. The main ForeSea model reaches only 13.6% IoU, and even stronger variants remain modest. This supports the claim that the task is hard, but it also limits the practical readiness implied by the forensic-search framing.

The main table emphasizes ForeSea, but ForeSea-Global and ForeSea-Hybrid often outperform it on overall temporal IoU and sometimes accuracy. The paper could better justify which variant is the primary contribution and how users should choose among them.

Some comparisons are not perfectly clean: different models have different capacities, input budgets, and retrieval settings, and several referenced baselines are recent or arXiv works. More standardized compute/frame budgets and clearer statistical uncertainty would strengthen the evidence.

The surveillance/forensic application raises privacy, misuse, and deployment concerns, but the manuscript provides little societal-impact analysis or guidance on responsible use, despite working directly with person-centric surveillance search.
